cues.text: Let us turn now to agility metrics and assessment.
We begin with a definition.
Business agility is the organisation's ability to sense change, make decisions and adapt effectively.
Notice the three verbs: sense, decide, adapt.
An agile organisation notices shifts in customers, markets, technology or regulation; it makes sound decisions about them without long delay; and it then changes how it works in response.
Business agility includes leadership, governance, product delivery, learning and operational responsiveness.
So it is not simply Scrum ceremonies.
Holding a daily stand-up or a sprint review does not, by itself, make an organisation agile.
Agility has to show up in how leaders steer, how governance approves and funds work, how products are delivered, how the organisation learns, and how quickly operations respond.
If agility is an ability, how do we know whether we have it?
We measure it, and we start with measures of time and flow.
First, lead time.
Lead time is the elapsed time from a request, or from some defined starting point, to delivery.
It is the customer's view of waiting.
Next, cycle time.
Cycle time is the time from when work commences to when it is completed.
It is the team's view of how long active work takes.
The source gives a warning about both: define exact measurement boundaries.
You must state precisely which event starts the clock and which event stops it.
If one team starts counting at the request and another at the start of work, their numbers cannot be compared.
Third, throughput.
Throughput counts completed work per period, for example items finished per week.
Fourth, work in progress, written WIP and pronounced "double-you eye pee".
WIP counts the items that are ongoing, started but not yet finished.
Fifth, predictability.
Predictability compares planned versus actual delivery, with awareness of uncertainty.
In other words, how closely did what we delivered match what we said we would deliver, remembering that plans are estimates and some variation is natural.
Now the measures that relate to software and service delivery.
Deployment frequency counts production deployments in a period, that is, how often changes are released into the live environment.
Change failure rate is the number of failed production changes divided by the total number of changes, multiplied by one hundred per cent.
Written out: change failure rate equals failed production changes over total changes, times 100 per cent.
Recovery time measures restoration after a service-impacting failure, so how long it takes to bring the service back once something has broken in a way users feel.
Escaped defects are defects that reach later stages or production, meaning they got past the checks that should have caught them.
Finally, team health reflects workload, autonomy, safety and collaboration.
This reminds us that sustainable agility depends on people, not only on numbers about delivery.
Let us work through the example.
A squad receives a request on Monday.
It starts the work on Wednesday and completes it on Friday.
We apply a consistent elapsed-day convention.
From Monday to Friday is 4 days, so lead time is 4 days.
From Wednesday to Friday is 2 days, so cycle time is 2 days.
The difference is the waiting between request and start, from Monday to Wednesday, which is queue time, 2 days.
Notice that lead time equals queue time plus cycle time: 2 plus 2 is 4.
Here half of the customer's wait was spent with nobody working on the request at all.
That is the kind of insight these measures reveal.
Now change failure rate.
In a month, 3 of 60 deployments cause failure.
Divide 3 by 60, which gives 0.05, and multiply by 100 to get 5 per cent.
So the change failure rate is 5 per cent.
Then recovery time.
Suppose recovery durations are 15, 30 and 45 minutes.
Add them: 15 plus 30 plus 45 is 90 minutes.
Divide by the 3 incidents and the mean is 30 minutes.
The source asks us to distinguish mean, median and tail behaviour.
The mean is the arithmetic average.
The median is the middle value when results are sorted, and the tail describes the slowest, worst cases, the rare long recoveries.
A mean can hide a few very long outages, and a median can hide them too, so looking at the tail matters when customers suffer most from the worst incidents.
Next, DORA delivery metrics.
DORA is pronounced "DOR-uh".
These metrics are a useful family of measures linking delivery throughput and instability.
Throughput on one side, instability on the other, so we see speed and stability together instead of trading one against the other blindly.
The source advises that you use the definitions applicable to your reporting, so be explicit about which definitions your organisation adopts.
Two cautions follow.
First, do not compare team velocity or story points across teams as a productivity league table.
Story points are a team's own relative estimates, so they are not a common unit across teams, and ranking teams by them distorts behaviour.
Second, measure service and customer outcomes, not individual activity.
What matters is whether services work and customers benefit, not how busy any one person appears.
Finally, assessment approaches.
The source names four: the Business Agility Health Radar from AgilityHealth, the SAFe Business Agility Assessment, the Spotify Squad Health Check, and the Agile Fluency diagnostic.
SAFe is pronounced "safe".
These approaches support structured reflection on capabilities, alignment, learning, delivery, teamwork and improvement.
They give teams and leaders a disciplined way to look at themselves.
Two principles govern their use.
A maturity score is a diagnostic, not proof of business value.
A high score does not demonstrate that the organisation is creating value; it only points to where to look.
And you should repeat assessments consistently, using the same approach, so changes over time are meaningful, and use the results to prioritise actions.
An assessment that does not lead to action is only a report.

To bring it together: agility is sensing, deciding and adapting; we measure it with clearly bounded flow, delivery and health measures; we interpret them with care; and we assess maturity as a diagnostic that guides improvement.
